And I believe General Lausic indicated he wanted to remove ambiguity. As part of the 92 ter process, he should remove that ambiguity right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... then perhaps you could ask him right away. Mr. Lausic, what you said during your interview, what you find as a text in your notebook, does that reflect that the way to prevent that heros of the homeland war would be put before a court was aiming at preventing that any behaviour would take place that could bring someone before a court. Is that how you intended ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, if you could move on to your next correction, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Same page and the same paragraph, 151. Again, it has to do with what Mr. Susak said at the briefing. I'm referring to the second line from the bottom: "Officials of political activity also must carry out their task by correctly briefing the members of the HV." Correction: "The officials of political activity also must carry out their task by correctly briefing [sic] the members of the HV." In Croatian "briefing" and "referiranje" do not mean the same thing, briefing and referiranje. So if I look at the translation, if I look at the Croatian version of my statement, it would seem that officials of political activity were supposed to report to soldiers but the meaning of the statement is -- by your leave, Mr. President, I'm going to convey things exactly as they stand in my diary; namely, Mr. Susak's words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The English reads "briefing" which is, as I understand, correct, in your view.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Then I have no objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lausic. Next correction, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Page 34, paragraph 157, line 4 from the bottom: "As far as I was concerned, traffic would go via the Maselinca Bridge and the way via Pag is free ..." In the transcript there is it no reference to "me," so as far as I'm concerned cannot be put in the context of this statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does that mean we should take out "as far as I'm concerned," just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you were looking for the next correction. My apologies. Mr. Lausic, if you could turn your attention to the next correction, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Page 35, paragraph 158, line three from the bottom: "The headquarters will be situated in the Ministry of the Interior and Mladen Laskovic ..." The wrong word was used or, rather, his last name was misspelled. It should be spelled L-a-c-k-o-v-i-c, not L-a-s-k-o-v-i-c.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please move to the next one, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Page 35, paragraph 161, line 2 from the bottom: "There was a discrepancy between the orders passed at the working meetings that were held and the way that these orders were implemented in the field." Correct. It would be correct in the following way: "The orders passed at the working meetings that had been held." In Croatian that would mean meetings that had been held, that had finished. They were held and then they were done; whereas the way it's been put here means that the meetings went on over a longer period of time, in continuity as it were. So the transcript has a correct reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. As far as my knowledge of the English language permits me to interpret this, that what the witness just said is reflected in the English text. Please proceed, next one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if I could -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, and if you asked for the English language. I think in fairness, and I don't know how important this is, that the meetings that were held could in fact refer to an ongoing process, the kinds of meetings that were held on a regular -- so I think that the correction that the witness made that is that meetings that had been held may offer a degree of precision that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that -- What do you consider what reflects better what you said the meetings that were held or that had been held? I understood you to say that the meetings that were held in a continuity that that's what you wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. The meetings were held and then orders were issued afterwards. Then, in the later period a discrepancy was observed in terms of what had been agreed upon at the meetings, what had been written into the orders, and then, ultimately, what was done in the field. So the meetings had been held.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So the meetings having been concluded, then what you saw in the field not in line, not fully in line, and there was some discrepancy. Then I misunderstood you. Thank you for correcting me. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lausic, I think you were moving on to your next correction.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Page 35, paragraph 162, line 7: "That the military police was not energetic enough in its actions and that we have to be more economical with the use of our resources and our equipment." Instead of the word "economical," the transcript refers to economising, that we have to economise with the use of our forces and equipment. In the Croatian meaning the word "economical" is different from the word "economising." Economising means good husbandry or, rather, taking care of a particular resource that you have in the right way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And which of the two now is ... is the correct version? Is that the part of what you just said is not yet on the transcript. I have some difficulties in repeating it. Is it -- "economical" I understand is in accordance with the economic laws, that is. And "economising" I do understand is to best deal with the available means and to use them in the -- I would say best way. Now, which is it? Is it "economizing" which is the right expression; or is it "economical?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Economizing would be right. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That means using them as a good house rather.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if you could continue, Mr. Lausic.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Again, page 35, paragraph 162, line 6 from the bottom: "During Flash, I used my eyes and ears. When I went out into the field, I saw that some things," et cetera et cetera. The correct version would be: "During Flash, I was missing eyes and ears in the field." Again, this is a rhetorical figure of speech. What I meant was that ... on the basis of the reports that I received, and later on, as I went out into the field, I observed many incorrect things. So what I missed were eyes and ears in the field. This is a rhetorical figure of speech. It is not that I used eyes and ears in the field, as this text states.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The English reads: "I was missing my ears an eyes on the ground," which I do understand is that you had no direct accurate information on what happened on the ground, until when you went there. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Page 37, paragraph 168 continues from page 36, line 5 from the bottom: "Units of the military police were fully subordinated to the commanders of the operative groups of the military districts or commanders of the operative groups, so -- or the highest commander." That's wrong. It should say the top commander. Well, the word that they meant was -- or, rather, what is written here has the connotation of supreme, whereas it should say the highest because it is the President of the Republic that is the Supreme Commander. That is the connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As I read it, Your Honour, in the portion, it does say highest instead of supreme.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Although, the context there were a few matters which may require proper attention. I will read to you slowly what it now says in English. It reads: "The units of the military police were in its entirety subordinated to the commanders of the Military Districts or the commanders of the Operative Groups or to the highest commander of the Croatian army, which was in accordance with the rules on the organisation and the work of the military police, which was issued in 1994." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Next one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no other corrections that I noted. However, due to the brevity of time that I had for studying this witness statement, well, I would like to remind you that I received all the documents on the 17th of December last year, so perhaps during the remaining part of my testimony, I may be able to indicate some other inaccuracies that may crop up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Have you read the statement in its entirety, since the 17th of December? I'm --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, correct. I have read it, but then my concentration went down too, because of the volume of the material that was submitted to me and also the fact that very little time was made available to me. I had to compare everything to the transcript, and this is rather a strenuous work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is your major concern about the comparison with the transcript? Is that where your hesitation lies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Precisely, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because if that is it the problem, if you come back at a later stage and point at some matter where you have doubts as whether it is transcribed properly, if it refers to the May interviews, of course, we'll have an opportunity to verify on the basis of the audio recording whether your present statement reflects what is you said. So if you have any problem in that respect in the near future, where you have some doubts, then there certainly will be a possibility to verify that. Do you have any other concerns, apart from the comparison with the audio recording and the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your question. No, I have no problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Then I suggest to the parties that if at a later stage anything would come up which is related to transcript and original language used, that this will be verified on the basis of the underlying material. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think this was implicit, Mr. Lausic, but I'll ask for purposes of the record. Was the information that you provided, and to the extent it may have been corrected today, during your interview and in your statement true and correct?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if asked about the same matters in court, would your answers be the same?

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: I believe that that is the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would move it into evidence. Mr. Misetic had a question about the interview, the August interview process that he wanted me to address after the break. I can do that before the break. And I don't know if it was supposed to be addressed outside the presence of the witness or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's what Mr. Misetic suggested.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I think it's a procedural matter that can be addressed with -- just before the break. I think we can handle it, so we don't interrupt --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps also for similar future situations, Mr. Lausic, do you speak and understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not to an extent to which that I could follow a conversation in English that employs expert terminology like it does before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have some basic knowledge of the English language. That is for all of us to know. Mr. Tieger, it is a procedural matter. I don't think that -- well, let me not speculate on anything. Would you like to raise the matter, and do you think it could be done in the presence of your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well based on what I -- I mean, it's difficult to know where this might go, and so I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then perhaps it would be wiser -- Mr. Lausic, there is a procedural matter we'd like to discuss, and since we do know where the discussion go, could I invite you to leave the courtroom for a short while.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I don't know if I was sufficiently clear. What I meant was at 12.25, if you wish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let now continue. We have set in action everything, so let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, I got a little bit out of sequence, and I apologise for my role in that. But in any event the question was Mr. Lausic's status at the time that he was -- the interview was taken, and I'm advised that he was regarded at that time as a witness, not a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm -- I don't know how to handle this and how to raise it, but in terms of the bases for the witness being changed from witness to suspect, and suspect to witness, and suspects again, this witness is a named identified member of the alleged JCE. That is public knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's a public filing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: My apologies for interrupting, Mr. Misetic. I think he is correct. There is no basis for do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's a mistake, or is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I can address it, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't whether you address whether Mr. Tieger made a mistake, but let's -- I will listen to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Okay. What happened was initially it was filed confidentially. The clarification identifying named individuals of the alleged JCE subsequently pursuant to a motion filed by Gotovina Defence and joined by the Markac Defence, the Trial Chamber ordered that that filing be made public. It, in fact, was publicly filed, so there nothing improper about discussing this publicly. Mr. Lausic is a named member of the alleged JCE in a filing by the Office of the Prosecutor. If he was a suspect in May of 2004 and he is he an identified member of the alleged JCE in, I believe, May of 2007, then what is the evidentiary basis for having changed him to a witness and removing the suspect classification, and then subsequently something must have arisen between August 2004 and May 2007, some additional evidentiary basis to make him a suspect again. I think that the matter needs further clarification because it may have a relevance to our cross-examination of this witness in terms what the Prosecution is alleging in terms of the role of the military police in this, the role of the witness in all of this, and I would like to put those matters to the witness in cross-examination. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe it presents any problem, Your Honour. I believe the filing indicated -- the clarification addressed those persons who may have been members of the JCE or may have been tools of the JCE. There were many matters that transpired between 2004 and the time of the filing, not the least of which was a clarification of the law with respect to tools and, no doubt, further exploration of the evidential material that might be relevant to those considerations. So I think as matters stand, the Defence is perfectly placed to make a determination about how to cross-examine the witness, and I can't imagine any further clarification would be of assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is my understanding that as recently as last week, and this is my understanding from Mr. Waespi, that in fact this witness was again advised of his rights under Rule 42 as a suspect. So if he's as late as last week -- as recently as last week being given his rights as a suspect under Rule 42, it is not simply a matter of he is a tool of the JCE but not his -- his witness status has remained intact since August of 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, first the facts, I do -- it's put to the Chamber that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued]... the witness was advised of his rights under Rule 42 as a suspect last week. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, it is not correct. In fact we didn't meet with the -- I think the communication was should we meet with the witness, we would do so. And it is correct that had we met with the witness to inquire about the statement, out of an abundance of caution, we would have advised the witness pursuant to Rule 42, but we did not. So, I mean, that distinction for purposes of this discussion may not be particularly pertinent. However, I have some considerable difficulty seeing the relevance to the issue before the Court. There's no question -- I mean, the Court has the information before it, knows when we filed the clarification, knows the status at the time. Our determination at this point to advise the witness under the broad, broad terms in the Rules that provide such advisement of rights to witnesses seems, to me, not to bear on issues related to cross-examination or any other relevant issues before the Court. Seems perfectly consistent with where we found ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to focus on one of the first questions. That is, what exactly the relevance for this information is. When cross-examining the witness what would it change? Because that's what Mr. Misetic raises, and that's what is contradicted by Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been given the floor but my learned friends on this matter. It is it classically important someone who is a suspect or a suspected accomplice or member of the criminal conspiracy or joint criminal enterprise is classically someone to whom the Court has to treat their evidence with caution. That is because their evidence may be self-serving, seek to put the blame on other people to avoid criminal liability themselves. And it is imperative that those listening to the evidence are able to bear that in mind when considering questions asked and the answers given of the witness. This is of great importance to those cross-examining because the manner of those questions should entitle the questioner to be able to reflect that position within the questions. Furthermore, certainly from the jurisdiction I come to and -- come from, and most other jurisdictions that I am aware of, this is a matter that the Prosecution should bear in mind when investigating and handling a witness in legal proceedings. They have a duty to fairness in the proceedings, and if a witness is not treated in the appropriate fashion of witnesses who come into this category of suspect or co-conspirator or accomplice, whatever, then they may be misled or mislead the Tribunal, and by that I mean courts, generally, into the nature of the evidence that is coming before it. Very important principle. It exists in many other jurisdictions and, we believe, of great importance to this witness, who was originally named within the proceedings as having been a member of the JCE. In my submission, it is not transparent to have a statement that the witness doesn't fall into that category, but a wider category. A tool of the JCE was another phrase used, and in my submission, that is being less than transparent with the position that the Court must appreciate in dealing with this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I can just respond, and then I'll let Mr. Tieger respond to both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I join in my colleague's position. Let me also add that I believe that it is clearly relevant in assessing the credibility of the witness that the Chamber know whether the witness has -- was told last week that he had rights under Rule 42 because it also goes directly to the motivation of any witness or -- who becomes a suspect given that answers to questions provided in his proceeding, he may perceive as putting him in jeopardy. And if that's the case, it's clearly a relevant factor for the Chamber in assessing credibility of answers and the credibility of the witness, and, therefore, I belive as part of cross-examination it is clearly a relevant factor to consider. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could just add something to that discussion of my learned friends. In our jurisdiction, I mean in Croatian jurisdiction where I come from, if one was interviewed in a capacity of suspect and then the status has been changed during the process and the suspects suddenly became a witness, then the interview in the capacity of suspect should not be entered into the evidence into the case file. So this is a principle of Croatian jurisdiction, and I believe this is the principle that the witness is simply used for because it's a common knowledge in Croatian judicial system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Two quick points, Your Honour. Of course, the Prosecution maintains its previous position. Number one, in response to -- one of the points Mr. Kay made, I fail to see how there is it any lack of transparency in merely reciting the terms of the clarification which is all that I did. If the Defence wants to argue on its own that the witness is or should be regarded as a member of the JCE rather than a tool, he is it free to do so. But all I did was recite the terms of the clarification to the best of my recollection. Number two, in terms of Mr. Misetic's inquiry, again, in the interest of full transparency, the witness was advised that if the -- if a further interview or proofing or further contact of that type was to go forward, he would be advised of his rights under Rule 42. Now I believe the Defence has all the information including the timing of the interviews, the timing of the filing of the clarification, and now we now the accuracy of the witness evidence. We also know what the Defence intends to argue, and they are free to do in terms of witness credibility or any other factors. But I don't -- I don't see any other issue to create a problem in going forward at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, the issue for us is the witness may have been told himself that he was a witness in 2004. I myself am now not exactly sure, given Mr. Tieger' comments, whether in fact OTP says he is a suspect or he is not a suspect. He seems to have been advised of his rights -- of the rights of a suspect last week, but there is a stopping short of saying he in fact is a suspect. It clearly goes to what was the witness told last week? What is the position of the Office of the Prosecutor, specifically on that point? And is it in the knowledge of this witness that he has that status? Let me clarify for the record what we have decided to argue, at least speaking for the Gotovina's Defence, in response to Mr. Tieger's comment is, has clearly not been decided and, of course, depends on what answers are to the questions. So I don't wish to in any way suggest that we have taken a position about what our position is going to be. That, of course, is it subject to hearing the testimony. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps first, a very factual question. And what was said to the witness last week, I did understand from Mr. Tieger that there had been no conversation. That he just expressed what he would have told him if there would have been a conversation or --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was an attempt to set up a meeting for the purpose of going over possible corrections and so forth. The witness was advised that if we met, he would be advised of his rights under Rule 42. That was the conversation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's -- now I better understand what happened and what did not happen. Mr. Kay, it must be something serious when are you holding your laptop in your hands. That must be really something ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's called first-aid where I come from. If I go back to the clarification filing by the Prosecution referred to by Mr. Tieger. And I will read out paragraph 1. "The Trial Chamber previously ordered the Prosecution to 'widen the circle' of named participants to include key military or political figures to the extent that they are known by the Prosecution. Although this was in the context of a JCE that embraced all persons whose conduct led to the commission of crimes, the Prosecution hereby complies with the order in the context of the proposed indictment by providing additional particulars concerning key military or political figures among the many persons who were members of the JCE. Alternatively, these persons were used by or cooperated with JCE members and their conduct is thereby imputable to the members of the JCE. These additional key military or political figures include the following people identified by reference to their position at the time of the events. This witness is thereafter named amongst others." Let us be frank, Your Honour. This is a witness who comes from an important position within the events that took place concerning the subject matter of this indictment. We all know that. This witness has made a statement and become a witness for the Prosecution. The Defence, it is it obvious, put this on the basis that he has made a self-serving statement. He has sought to cooperate with the Prosecution to avoid prosecution himself, and that his evidence is unreliable for those reasons. It is of paramount importance that the Court be absolutely clear as to the nature of this witness that appears before it, and that the usual safeguards that can happen in all cases are available to the Defence in relation to this witness. It is something we would be seeking. His statement has now been through the 92 process, put into -- sought to be put into evidence before the Court, and in those circumstances at that stage when we have this title of evidence, we are entitled to know and the Court to be informed of the exact position with this witness. It is it utterly wrong for there to be a clouding of the issue; could be a tool, or is a member supported, contributed to the JCE, because that, in our submission, is an attempt to play fast and loose with the usual norms of save guards in relation to evidence from a particular category of witness. It serves the Prosecution interest, but it does no service to the Defence, and, in our submission, also the Court, because the Court has to direct itself appropriately in relation to the reliability of witnesses. And one can see every reason why a suspect cautioned gives a self-serving interview, is then ushered through a process whereby he becomes a witness because he is extended the hand that he will not be prosecuted, if he cooperates. And we have to be absolutely clear about matters such as these because they involve evidence that is very fundamental to the charges against all the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Very briefly. It also raises the implication for the witness under the circumstances as to his potential to be able to seek counsel. He is, under the circumstances, potentially liable to be prosecuted in Croatia, and he, for the witnesses basis, is entitled to know what his particular rights are under the circumstances. And I don't know if that has been communicated to the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very practical. A question is put to the Prosecution: Is this witness considered by the Prosecution to be a suspect member of the joint criminal enterprise; or is he considered to be a tool, I think that's the -- you wanted clarity on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, there is it one additional point that I failed to make, and I'm reminded of by Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but I'm now putting a few questions, and if there's anything you'd like to add, I will certainly give you an opportunity. But let's not --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from what Mr. Kehoe --

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: It's actually important, Mr. President because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll let you continue in one or two sentences to make clear how important it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: The issue is in the change of status from suspect to witness, what was the discussion, if any, that may have been relayed to the witness about a change in status? Because to the extent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can ask Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So one of the questions, Mr. Tieger, you're invited to respond, is whether you consider Mr. Lausic to be a participant in a joint criminal enterprise, at least as it was clarified, whether you consider him to a potential member of the joint criminal enterprise, or a potential instrument, a tool.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, I'm not going to deviate, and I don't think it would be appropriate to at this point, from the clarification that the Court at that time asked us to file and which we did file and which Mr. Kay just recited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say he is either a participant --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... and we filed a formal pleading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And now, therefore, you disagree with Mr. Kay in being in a position at this moment to -- to provide further clarity in this respect. You say he is either one of the two, and that's what the Prosecution is able to say, was willing to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's precisely what we said in -- in the clarification, and it hasn't been changed since.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, let me then very practically ask the Defence, you have expectations of what the Chamber should do. But let me first address the other matter raised by Mr. Misetic which -- because I had forgotten. Was Mr. Lausic informed about a change of in status when he was interviewed in August?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In August 2004, Your Honour, you know where I was at the time. I don't know the answer to that, but I do know that his -- I'm advised that his counsel was present. That's about the -- that's about the most information I can provide at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In 2004 counsel was present, you say. Le me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at the cover page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would that be Nika Pinter, or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: That is it his counsel. However, I'm a bit confused, and I think that may be confused as well. Because as we know the substance of the statement is from the May 2004 suspect interview, in most respects. There may be additions that took place in August. But the statement itself indicates that the interview was taken on three days in August and makes no reference to the questioning in May, so I'm wondering whether the indication that Ms. Pinta was present refers to potentially the fact that she was present for the suspect interview in may, and whether or not she was present in August is unclear it me at this point. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I think can I clarify that confusion. I'm advised that it's both. That's what I was -- that's what I was advised. I can double check that, but I'm ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Indeed, there's a strong suggestion that if the dates of the interview are the 9th, the 10th, and the 11th of August, and names of all persons present during interviews that that would relate to the interviews mentioned here. But Mr. Tieger will verify that, I take it, and that we even could each ask the witness. What exactly would the Defence like the Court to do in very practical terms apart from giving the traditional guarantees? Just what would you invite us to do? To explain to the witness what the situation is; that is, that he was once interviewed as a suspect, that at a later stage he was -- and we could ask him how he experienced this position. The presence of the counsel was interviewed, but primarily as a witness, and then to tell him that the -- perhaps the objective grounds for -- or at least that -- that the grounds for considering him a suspect at the time might not have disappeared in the their entirety so that we are still in a position where, of course, it also depends on the answers he may give. Someone -- if you'd say, My evidentiary basis to consider him a suspect are insufficient. But, of course, he can change that himself and, therefore, to say that is he not -- if there would be any answer, he would have fear to incriminate himself that he is not under an obligation to answer that question. He might come up with totally new information as a follow-up of the -- of -- in response to the questions put to him. What exactly, what kind of action -- and I'm not saying that the Chamber will follow your suggestions. But what would you expect the Chamber to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I will let Mr. Kuzmanovic deal with the second portion of it. The first question, Your Honour -- and I still don't -- I mean, we got into a discussion about JCE, a member or a tool. The issue from my perspective is very simple. Does the OTP consider him a suspect or not? I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But then -- we have at least a couple of concepts of a suspect is. For example, is someone still a suspect if not every basis for a suspicion doesn't exist anymore, but where there is a firm and irreversible decision not to further pursue the matter and not to prosecute him. Would he still be a suspect? That is one of the questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: We litigated that issue in January of 2008. The position of the Office of the Prosecutor at that time was, Yes, indeed, he is a suspect. I would say Your Honour that suspect is strictly defined in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. And the ultimate question is, is this a person concerning whom the Prosecutor possesses reliable information which tends to show that the person may have committed a crime over which the Tribunal has jurisdiction? It's not an assertion that the person should be accused. It's may have. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, should be accused. If he cannot be accused anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: You will recall that that's the position that we took in January, and the Office of the Prosecutor fought us tooth and nail on that position, and we had to come up with a comprise to resolve that matter. But as far as I understand, the Office of the Prosecutor made submissions to the Chamber that despite the fact that the OTP can no longer indict the person, the person remains a suspect because they could face jeopardy in the states of the Former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore, if we're talking about suspect and if you're referring to the Rules, of course, you're refer to what -- and I heard that before. You're referring to a mechanism what is usually called an intrastate or a intra-institutional mechanism, and that sometimes, although the rationale for protecting someone from self-incrimination which may not any further apply in one institution, does not exclude for once and forever the possibility that treating him not as a suspect could create a risk that unaware of possible prosecutions in other jurisdictions that this would be not appropriate to do. So then we have someone for which perhaps an objective test would still qualify -- he would still qualify as a suspect here, although there is no way of any following prosecution and that there's no way of any further investigation against that person, wherever he may be, at some risk, and I would like to know from you whether ever any investigation has been conducted against Mr. Lausic in view of possible prosecution in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well, I obviously wouldn't have access to that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, you can ask whether you are aware of such -- either you -- you would know would, of course, not be an absolute answer whether there ever has been an investigation, but you could tell us whether you are aware of any such investigation that was ever conducted or you're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it, Your Honour. But let me say this, just so that I'm clear and I don't get accuse of taking two sides on the same issue. What I'm relaying to you is what I understand the Office of the Prosecutors's position to have been in January 2008. That is to say, we were the ones, you will recall to you, who raised the issue of these -- when they were trying to do suspect interviews with persons in the Split Military District chain of command, we said that, in fact, the use of suspect status as a means of coercing and pressuring people. The Office of the Prosecutor came back and said they're still faced jeopardy in the countries of the former Yugoslavia. There are still, as I understand it, and Mr. Tieger will know more about it, cooperation between Office of the Prosecutor and local prosecutors in terms of exchange of evidence and those type of matters, and that for that reason, these persons were been given suspect status. It's relevant for a number of reasons because the witness should know either if is he a suspect from the perspective of the Office of the Prosecutor, that has certain implications on his testimony. If the Prosecution is going to come forward and say, Mr. Lausic, the Prosecution no longer considers you a suspect, that may actually be relevant to the witness in terms of the answers he will provide in light of the fact that the statement that is now before you is, in fact, given at a time when he was a suspect, at least major -- the majority of it was. Which portions came in August is not clear from the face of the statement. But either way, the issue has relevance here, and we -- you know, to me, it seems rather simple to say, Given that the Prosecution has already said that the fact that someone can no longer be indicted here doesn't have an impact on the definition of suspect under the Rules of Procedure, whether Mr. Lausic fits that definition in the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, last round.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Certainly, Your Honour. The Prosecution is not a proponent of what the rules say. The Prosecution was doing its best in the circumstance that Mr. Misetic described as we related to the Defence to abide by the Rules as best it could interpret them, and we offered that interpretation which seemed to be consistent with what we understood. I have already indicated in this particular context that we indicated to the witness that should we meet for the purpose of going over the statement, that we would advise him of his rights pursuant to Rule 42. I think the Court has had all the information it needs to proceed for quite some time now. I would be happy to answer any explicit questions the Court might have. But it seems to me that much of the -- much of the last few minutes has been taken up with various possibilities that will be addressed during the course of cross-examination. And all the relevant factors are now before the Court, and that is the basis on which all of this has been argued.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I tried one again. Mr. Kuzmanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I guess the bottom line really is, what is the status of this particular witness? The Chamber is entitled to know, we're entitled to know. What incentives, if any, has this witness be given to testify under the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is clear, and it was already clear from the foregoing. One minute for practical suggestions because I asked that before. What do you expect the Chamber to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, we would be grateful if you could, after the break, ask the witness -- either first instruct the witness, as I understand Mr. Tieger's position, that he is considered a suspect. That's point one, and that's why he was advised of his rights under Rule 42, unless I'm wrong, but that's how I understood the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I understood it a bit differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm now asking for the practical suggestion and not reopening the debate. To instruct the witness, to at least to tell what the situation is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes. The fact is that if the three parties in this proceeding: The Trial Chamber, the Prosecution, and the Defence cannot determine whether or not the person is a suspect, I can imagine that the witness, himself, is having system difficulty coming to that conclusion. And I would urge all of us to come to a -- a resolution of that issue and to advise the witness of it. Because in addition to what Mr. Kuzmanovic said that the witness has certain rights under the Rules if indeed he is a suspect, there is also the issue of the witness's -- the assessment of his credibility that the Chamber will have to make. The second thing is I would be grateful if the chamber would inquire of the witness simply if he has any or had any communications considering his status and what was told to him about, again, if anything, about changes of status from suspect to witness and if anything was expected of him as a result of that change in status. Was he advised that he would become a witness in the case against the three accused here? Did he, under whatever circumstances, perhaps under his own conclusions that may not have been put him by the Prosecution, come to the understanding that there was some quid pro quo in exchange for the change in status and that doesn't -- again, let me be clear that I'm not asserting that anything was done like that by the Prosecution, but given the circumstances, did the witness come to that conclusion as a result of the change in -- in status that occurred apparently over -- somewhere within a four-month period? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: An order from the Court to the Prosecution directing them to inform the Court when Mr. Lausic moved from the status of being a suspect to becoming a witness, an order from the Court to the Prosecution to declare any statements they have made to the witness about him becoming a witness. My submission is that from what Mr. Tieger has said, he is a suspect. That is why it was in the Prosecution's mind to caution him. In those circumstances, I submit that his 92 ter submission through the Prosecution should no longer be accepted. He should be taken as a viva voce witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What in this respect changes your position in relation to the earlier --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My position is this: That I'm highly concerned about the unsatisfactory nature of the status of this witness, and the more that has been discussed, the more the alarm bells have rung in my head as counsel for one of the accused about the nature of this witness and the type of testimony that has been obtained from him at this stage. In my submission, there is it every incentive for that statement to have been self-serving. I think the revelation that he was going to be cautioned this week before being spoken to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I asked you what we should do, and we're now more or less ending up in repeating some of the arguments that were raised. And that is not what I have invited you to do at this very moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought Your Honour wanted me to explain my change in position. I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... if you would say it's on the basis of the discussions we had today, then that is clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kuzmanovic, very short question. Because we have to take a break. What specifically are at this moment the rights for this witness different from any other witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: In this particular case if is he a suspect, Your Honour, I think he is entitled to know that he has the right to counsel and to have that counsel present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we find the right of counsel for a suspect who appears as witness in court?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we knew that before the witness testified, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. But I'm asking you where to find that in the Rules. That the witness testifies under ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: I would think under the practical circumstances given the fact that he is subject to prosecution in Croatia, he would be entitled to that. Ans I can't cite a specific rule in our rules right now, Your Honour, but I think under the circumstances, he would be entitled to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The right to be informed that if any answer would incriminate himself --

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: I was going to direct you to Rule 90(E), Mr. President. The witness would clearly have rights to object and that he would be given use immunity by the Chamber in that event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of those Rules. We have to take a break now later than we intended to do. Could the witness be informed that we would like to see him back after the break, and we'll resume at five minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be brought into the courtroom. The Chamber will put a few questions to the witness before we proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, before we continue, I would like to put a few -- before we continue, I'd like to put a few procedural questions to you. A statement was taken, I do understand, in May 2004, a statement which has been video-recorded, and you referred to the recording several times. You were then assisted by counsel, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then you were informed that this was an interview where you were a suspect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you were interviewed again in August 2004. We see on the cover page that same counsel was present. Was she present both in May and in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, in August, was -- was explained whether you still were a suspect or that you would -- were interviewed as a witness. Has this been explained to you in August?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some time towards the end -- well, I'm speaking from memory now. Towards the end of July 2004, I was contacted by telephone, by my lady lawyer, and she conveyed a message to me from the OTP from The Hague, that I had been taken off the list of suspects, and that the Prosecutors were asking for another meeting with me, and they were asking what the right time for that would be, but in a different status, as a witness. At that interview, the transcript that -- the transcript of the interview that I gave as a suspect would be transformed into a witness statement. I agreed to that. The time was set, and the investigators came to Zagreb on the mentioned date, and, at the Office of The Hague Tribunal in The Hague in the presence of my lawyer, Mrs. Nika Pinter, I gave a witness statement. This was done in the following way: The investigators read the transcript in the English version with the assistance of an interpreter. They repeated what was said during my interview, and then, at the end of these two or three days, if I'm not mistaken, of this interview, an English witness statement was compiled, and I signed every page. After August 2004, I had no further contacts with The Hague Tribunal, with the OTP, or with anyone else, all the way up to December --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll come to December, I take it December 2008. You just told us that you -- a message was revealed to you that you were taken off the list of suspects and that was without any conditions, then, I do understand. It was not, You have to give a statement, and then we'll take you off the list of suspects; or was it just revealed to as a message, You are taken off the list of suspects, and you're invited to have another meeting. Were you under any obligation at the time to have another meeting, or were you, just as I just said, invited for that other meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my understanding was that this was my moral obligation, if I can put that way, to come to that meeting. I did not even put that question to myself as to whether I had to come or whether I didn't have to come. I simply accepted this as a fact, and I was ready to respond to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So you were invited, and you responded in the positive.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it from your previous answers that you were not offered anything in return for cooperating or at least meeting again with the investigators?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now we come to December 2008. I take it, then you were -- could you briefly explain what happened then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some time after the 10th of December - I don't have the exact date recorded - I received a call through the interpreter at The Hague OTP, and I was asked to come, on the 17th of December, to the Office of The Hague Tribunal in Zagreb. Mr. Foster, an investigator, would then hand me over the Croatian translations of the transcript of the meeting that I had in May 2004 as a suspect, and a Croatian translation of my witness statement from August 2004. At the agreed time, at exactly 1600 hours, I was at the Office of The Hague Tribunal. Mr. Foster came, accompanied by a Prosecutor whose first name was Stefan; I can't remember his last name. He took this binder out of his bag. He handed it over to me. He handed over two CDs as well with the video and audio recordings from May 2004. He warned me that we could not discuss the case at all. He said that this was simply a technical hand-over of the documents concerned and the two CDs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Were you then invited to meet again with them, or was it just that the material was given to you for review?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The material was given to me for a review. And then last week -- I can't be very specific because I don't have my notes here with me. Last week I received a telephone call from The Hague OTP, and it was agreed that on the 21st of January, 2009, Mr. Foster accompanied by Prosecutor Tieger would come to Zagreb and then they would go through my witness statement together with me. I agreed to that. However, on the 20th of January, a day before they were due to arrive, I was contacted yet again by the OTP. Again, everything I'm saying takes place through an interpreter, and I was cautioned that this meeting that had been agreed upon for the 21st of January would be recorded. There would be an audio and video recording. I was cautioned that this was compulsory for The Hague OTP on the basis of Article 42 of the Rules of Procedure of The Hague Tribunal. I was told that I have the right to have an attorney present. I asked for an opportunity to consult my attorney. I did indeed consult my attorney over the telephone, and he cautioned me that Article 42 pertains to suspects -- suspect interviews, and that this is by no means a form that was applied in the form of witness interviews. When I talked to The Hague Tribunal again, I said I that agreed to an interview but without any audio or video recording, and that I do not see any need for my lawyer to be present. After my response to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Oh, sorry, there it goes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After my response that effect, again through an interpreter, I was asked to give the telephone number of my lawyer so that the Prosecutions from The Hague would explain to my lawyer why this was necessary. I said that there was no need for them to establish any contact with my lawyer. I said that I was sufficiently well versed from a legal point of view with the work and the Rules involved, and that they could explain to me why it was necessary for the lawyer to be there and for a video and audio recording. I was told that there was a possibility of a necessity on the part of the Croatian judiciary for an audio an video recording of this interview of ours where I would be shown some new documents that I would state my views on. I refused that kind of interview. And after that, the gentleman from The Hague OTP said that there was no need for them to come to Zagreb and that we would be seeing each other in Court today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Could I ask you, your interview was about -- and your statements are about what happened in a period before Operation Storm but also about the time when Operation Storm took place, what functions you had, what meetings you attended, et cetera. So it covers the Operation Storm and the pre-Operation Storm period. Was this ever investigated in Croatia, as far as you were aware of, in view of establishing whether you would be a suspect under Croatian law for whatever offence committed in this context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before the Croatian judiciary, I was not given any sort of status of suspect in respect of any of the events in Croatia save for one case that was conducted in Croatia against Generals Ademi and Norac, where I appeared as a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you were never informed or you never concluded from any circumstance that you would be investigated as a suspect, in relation to these matters; that is, your involvement in your professional capacity in Operation Storm and what preceded that operation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lausic, are you aware that no new indictments can be brought against persons anymore before this Tribunal, apart from -- I have to be more precise. No further indictments in cases relating to, well, the 1990s to say so. So I'm not talking about perjury cases or contempt cases. But are you aware that no indictments can be brought anymore before this tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, Mr. President. I am aware of that. I have to add to what I said concerning my contacts with representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor which transpired last week in respect of their intention to come to Zagreb. When I opposed the audio an video recording and the presence of lawyer, they warned me and told me that they could not and would not be issuing an indictment against me. However, that they had obligations toward the Croatian judiciary in the sense that where certain proceedings would be initiated against me, they would have to have that sort of recording of an interview conducted with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any concern about investigations or proceedings brought against you in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not have any concerns in that respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you, when interviewed in 2004, in May, later in August, were your answers ever influenced by any concern you may have had at that time to be prosecuted before this Tribunal or to be prosecuted in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To hold the status of a suspect is psychologically speaking, of course, a more difficult position than that of a witness. By the same token, the degree of concern and preparedness before giving a statement is different to the situation where one give a statement as a witness. I have to say that as a police officer of a long-standing, I interpreted it as a tactical move on the part of the OTP where in that first contact with me, they gave me the status of a suspect. However, with the same degree of conscientiousness and seriousness were the answers that I have regardless of whether my status was that of a suspect or a witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So when you testified this morning when we had gone through the August 2004 statement when you said, I gave the answers to the best of my abilities in accordance with the truth, that is valid -- was valid at the time and is valid today. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then having gone through all these details, Mr. Lausic, whatever we discussed, whether you can still be indicted, which is not the case, before this Tribunal, and whether you have any concerns about what might be investigated in Croatia. You told us that you had no concerns. But, nevertheless, I inform you that, under the Rules of this Tribunal, that if a question would be put to you and if an answer to that question, a truthful answer to that question, might tend to incriminate you, that you may object against answering that question. That should be clear to you. I take it that as a policeman you know what I'm saying, that this is the reflection of -- of your right to be protected against forced self-incrimination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is it clear, then, Mr. Tieger, you may proceed. We have not much time left, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I should probably begin by tendering 65 ter 7032 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's the 92 ter statement August 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections. No objections. Then Mr. Registrar that would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P2159, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P2159 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And similarly for the accompanying --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. May I take it are they put on a list already, and there's, of course, seven documents were added to -- at least you seek them to be added to your 65 ter list. Is there any objection against the seven documents not yet on the 65 ter list? Then leave is granted to add any document appearing in your application to add it to the 65 ter list. Then, finally, was there any objections exceeding the word limit as we found it in the motion of the Prosecution? If not, then permission is granted to that. Is there any objection against admission of any of the documents appearing on -- attached -- appearing in the motion, the 92 ter motion? Then we can prepare the list, and they are admitted into evidence. But numbers, of course, still have to be assigned to them. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, P2159, which is the August 1994 [sic] statement refers at paragraph 19 to the creation of temporary instructions for the work of the military police units and then again at various paragraphs to the establishment of the rules on the organisation and work of the military armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd like to turn to that document. That's Exhibit 880 [sic], and if that can be presented to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, you should see the rules governing the structure and operation of the military police of the armed forces of Croatia on the screen right now. That's P1880. And I'd like to turn first to Article 9. Now, Article 9 states that: "While performing their regular military police tasks, military police units are subordinate to the commander of the Military District. The commander of the HRM, the Croatian navy; the commander of the HRZ, the Croatian air force; or to the highest HV commander by function in the military police units of operations." And if I can direct your attention to paragraph 28 of the statement. That is, paragraph 28 of P2159, it states that at item 9 of these rules: "The commanders of the military police units are subordinated in their daily operative command to the commanders of the Military Districts, to the air force commanders, the navy, or to the highest commander in their area of responsibility." Mr. Lausic, I wanted to ask you when you used the term "daily operative command" in your statement at paragraph 28, did that mean anything different from the language in Article 9 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Probably best not lead the witness on to the interpretation of the statement but to ask him what he meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm inclined here that -- well, we could start with that, Mr. Tieger, and then later come to any linguistic issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If I may make my objection again. The tactic of putting things to a witness and then drawing his attention to something else is in and of itself leading. I will object now and to the extent that practice is going to continue to be used, it is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A question without any direction isn't a question anymore. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger, and please keep in mind that you perhaps first ask the witness for an explanation of what he meant, and if there is any need then to further address the linguistic issue, then you are you free to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, referring to paragraph 28 of your statement, what did you mean when you stated that the commanders of the military police units are subordinated in their daily operative command to the commanders of the Military Districts? Can you clarify and explain that to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: MATE LAUSIC
utterances.text: Article 9 of the Rules governing the organisation and work of the military police which is the full title of the rules dating from 1994 -- or, rather, Article 8 states that all units of the military police are subordinated to the military police administration under the command and control of the chief of the military police administration. This is implied in Article 8 and that something that was in the course of 1992 and subsequently explained in various instructions, it implies that the administration of the Military Police which is part of the Ministry of Defence in organisational terms and is found in the sector of the security intelligence affairs of the MOD headed by the minister of security in the first instance, and by the minister, himself, in the second instance, was not part of the Main Staff of the armed force of the Republic of Croatia. Article 8 implies that the military police administration shall determine the basis of development of the military police through various specialities and subspecialities, that it shall follow the implementation of any such development, that it shall advance the organisation and structure of the military police, that the military police administration shall develop educational curricula for the training of the military police, that the military police administration shall determine the criteria for the selection of common policemen, non-commissioned and commissioned officers. In other words it shall be in charge of the personnel matters within the administration, that through the personnel administration of the Ministry of Defence, it shall appoint and relieve of duty the command cadre, that it shall enforce the control and monitor the work of the military police, that it shall issue the military police with the necessary orders and instructions on the tactics aimed at implying -- at implementing various tasks. In other words, to command the units of the military police at a strategic level, with the objective of achieving a uniform tactics of work and uniform application or implementation of military police powers. Article 9, which reads that while performing regular military police tasks, military police units shall be subordinate to the commander of the Military District, the commander of the Croatian navy, the commander of the Croatian air force, or to the highest Croatian army commander by function in the military police units area of operations means that all these bodies listed in Article 9 within which area of responsibility given military police units are deployed, be it a battalion, company, or a platoon, shall have the power to issue daily operational orders to carry out all the military police tasks falling within the purview of the military police. The subsequent Articles of the rules list the relevant tasks and powers of the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, your timing is impeccable. It is it precisely 1345, the time that Court likes to close.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lausic, we'll adjourn for the day. I'd like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in any way with anyone about the testimony, testimony whether given already today or testimony still to be given in the days to come, and we'd like to see you back tomorrow, when we're sitting in the afternoon. We adjourn, and we resume on Tuesday, the 27th of January, quarter past 2.00 in the afternoon, in Courtroom I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
